extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty and administrators responsible for assessing/ improving undergraduate programs and evaluating teaching (including faculty conducting class visits and peer review)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing student learning and teaching in undergraduate mathematics programs, including procedures for class visits, peer review of teaching, setting learning goals, designing strategies, selecting assessment methods, and running an assessment cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of class visits for junior faculty evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Early in the semester the two faculty members meet and go over the course syllabus; two or sometimes three consecutive classes are visited as part of department evaluation under college guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After visits, the senior colleague conveys a written evaluation to the junior colleague with a copy to the department chair; visits follow a formal structure and are part of departmental evaluation of junior faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put observations into context
rubrics_metrics.description: In the discussion following a visit, it is important to put observations into context so that apparent problems (e.g., an inadequate answer or awkward exchange) may be understood in light of what happened in previous sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a question had been addressed previously, or whether a student-teacher exchange reflected prior incidents; lack of context can lead to misleading evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of the written class-visit report
rubrics_metrics.description: The write-up includes a general description of the class, specific comments both positive and negative, and the suggestions or ideas discussed after the visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This letter becomes part of the junior faculty member’s file; include sufficient detail to justify recommendations and provide actionable suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junior faculty visits to senior faculty classes are non-evaluative
rubrics_metrics.description: Visits by junior faculty to senior faculty classes are less structured and are intended to foster discussion of teaching, sharing ideas, and constructive criticism rather than formal evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such visits are encouraged but not required; follow-up is typically informal and junior faculty may be uncomfortable criticizing seniors—expect less formal reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visit findings to inform teaching practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty should consider observers’ suggestions and may change teaching style or technique (e.g., tone, quiz policies, classroom interactions) while retaining autonomy over final decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate suggestions consistent with instructor personality; trial changes and solicit student feedback (example: changing strict quiz collection policy after reflecting on classroom atmosphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of classroom visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Classroom visits see only a few classes and the presence of a visitor can affect student behavior and class dynamics, especially in smaller classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize sampling limitations; consider multiple visits or complementary data sources; allow the observed teacher to decide whether to introduce visitors or have them remain unobtrusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announced vs. unannounced visitor presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher being observed should decide whether to introduce visitors, explain their presence, invite them to participate, etc.; unobtrusive visits may produce 'purer' observations while announced visits involve students and the process more directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the advantage of more natural observation against the benefit of transparency and student inclusion in the evaluation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way exchange of class visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Structuring class visits as a two-way street (junior visiting senior and vice versa) fosters discussion and mutual learning but may be limited by tenure ratios and workloads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reciprocal visits where feasible to broaden perspectives; ensure the practice does not impose unreasonable burden on junior faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer visitation team composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A peer visitation team usually consists of three observers: one from within the department and two from outside the department (or otherwise a mix of disciplinary backgrounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include observers with diverse perspectives and with interest or previous experience in evaluating teaching to provide a variety of viewpoints on teaching effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review visit schedule and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers visit the class at least twice during the term, with all observers present for each visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple visits help triangulate observations over time; schedule to avoid major events and provide observers with background materials between visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-visit briefing and provision of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the first visit, the faculty member meets with the observers to inform them of course history and provides written materials such as syllabi, assignments, and samples of student writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make teaching goals explicit and supply context so observers interpret classroom events in light of course design and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation logistics and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers may arrive early to chat with students or observe interactions, sit in different parts of the room to capture different vantage points, and stay after class to speak with students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use body placement and brief student interactions strategically to observe engagement levels; ensure methods respect student consent and privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-visit debrief and immediate instructor meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty member should meet with the observers immediately after the visit to give context to the observations and discuss interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate instructor background into observers' reports where relevant; immediate debriefs reduce misinterpretation of isolated events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observer report writing
rubrics_metrics.description: After the visit, each observer writes a report of what was observed, either in a self-chosen format or on a departmentally constructed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the review is informal, allow flexible formats to capture diverse insights; for official processes use uniform formats to aid comparability; reports may be combined or submitted separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observers meeting with the instructor
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers may meet with the faculty member to discuss their observations, either as a group or individually, to elaborate findings and recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these meetings to clarify misunderstandings, provide actionable suggestions, and help the instructor plan changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of peer review reports in teaching portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Together with student work and student evaluations, peer review reports can provide a fuller view of an instructor’s classroom work for a teaching portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat peer reports as one component of a broader evidence base documenting teaching effectiveness and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review benefits: multiple perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Having several observers in the class at the same time allows multiple perspectives on the class and brings discipline-diverse expectations and insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including observers from other disciplines can enrich subsequent discussions on teaching strategies and student engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review success factors and challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is labor intensive and time-consuming (scheduling, writing reports); in institutions without established peer review, persuasion and faculty development are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate logistic challenges, time commitments, and the need for training in sensitive observation and commenting; build departmental consensus to reduce risk of misuse or political bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding misuse and abuse of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the misuse and abuse that opponents worry about, there needs to be some consensus in a department so the practice is seen as a departmental effort to help students learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide faculty development workshops to train observers in objective and sensitive commenting; clarify purpose and procedures publicly to students and faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative peer evaluation method: instructor absent + focus groups
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative form of peer evaluation is having a faculty member visit the class with the instructor absent and hold focus group discussions with the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See referenced work (Patricia Shure) for details; this method emphasizes student perspectives but changes the observation dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment purpose: three core questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment activity should answer: (1) What should our students learn? (2) How well are they learning? (3) What should we change so future students will learn more and understand it better?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to frame the entire assessment cycle and to connect goals, measurement, and improvement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle (a): match objectives to institutional and student contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives should be realistically matched to institutional goals as well as to student backgrounds, abilities, aspirations, and professional needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align program expectations with institutional mission and realistic student capabilities to ensure feasible and relevant assessment targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle (b): focus assessment on mathematics curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: The major focus of assessment (by mathematics departments) should be the mathematics curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize evaluation of curricular content, sequencing, and coherence when designing department assessment plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle (c): integrate assessment with program review
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should be an integral part of the academic program and of program review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make assessment ongoing and connected to program-level decision-making rather than an isolated activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle (d): use assessment to improve teaching for all students
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should be used to improve teaching and learning for all students, not to filter students out of educational opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessment to support improvement and inclusivity rather than gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle (e): involve and inform students and faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Students and faculty should be involved in and informed about the assessment process, from the planning stages throughout implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage stakeholders early, clarify purposes and uses of data, and report results back to participants in a timely fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle (f): collect data for predetermined purposes and report promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Data should be collected for specific purposes determined in advance, and the results should be reported promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid collecting irrelevant data; plan analyses and dissemination methods before collection to ensure timely use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment cycle step 1: articulate learning goals and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate the learning goals of the mathematics curriculum and a set of objectives that should lead to the accomplishment of those goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move from general program goals to specific course and assessment goals; align goals with institutional mission and general education requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment cycle step 2: design strategies to accomplish objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Design strategies (e.g., curriculum and instructional methods) that will accomplish the objectives, taking into account student learning experiences and diverse learning styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify which curricular elements and assignments target each goal and ensure strategies allow measurement of progress over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment cycle step 3: determine areas and methods of assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the areas of student activities and accomplishments in which quality will be judged and select assessment methods designed to measure student progress toward completion of objectives and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign responsibility for each assessment area and select methods matched to the type of learning to be measured (combine multiple methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment cycle step 4: gather, summarize, and interpret assessment data
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather assessment data; summarize and interpret the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate analytic approaches to translate raw data into actionable findings; ensure timely reporting to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment cycle step 5: use results to improve the program
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the results of the assessment to improve the mathematics major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement curricular and instructional changes based on evidence, then monitor effects in subsequent assessment cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider when setting learning goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors: institutional mission, background of students and faculty, facilities, and degree program goals should be considered when setting learning goals of the mathematics major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align departmental goals with institutional mission and practical constraints; incorporate expectations about writing, job skills, and graduate preparation as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local information to analyze (faculty, students, facilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the nature of faculty, students, courses, and facilities; consider questions such as expectations and special needs of students, why/how students learn, faculty teaching styles, special talents of faculty, available facilities, and representativeness of majors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this local analysis to identify special opportunities or constraints that affect achievable learning goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program goals and general education alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree program goals should incorporate general education objectives (e.g., graduates speak and write with precision; gain scientific literacy; apply knowledge) and prepare students for employment, further study, or meaningful lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mathematics program goals complement and reinforce broader institutional learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of curricular threads or themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic or thematic threads (e.g., mathematical reasoning, communication, computing, modeling) are valuable for articulating measurable objectives and giving curriculum unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define threads across courses so each contributes to progress along the theme and assessment can track cumulative development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal example: mathematical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to perform complex tasks; explore subtlety; discern patterns, coherence, and significance; undertake intellectually demanding mathematical reasoning; and reason rigorously in mathematical arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design course activities and assessments that require higher-order reasoning and proof construction rather than rote computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal example: personal potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to undertake independent work, develop new ideas, discover new mathematics, possess advanced critical sophistication, motivation, and attitudes required for further study and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities for independent projects, research experiences, and tasks that cultivate initiative and creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal example: nature of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should understand breadth of mathematical sciences, interconnecting principles, interplay among applications, problem-solving, and theory, and be able to write proofs and appreciate historical/contemporary contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include content and assignments that expose students to both theoretical and applied aspects and historical perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal example: mathematical modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should apply mathematics to complex problems; formulate and solve problems; undertake real-world modeling projects; use computers for simulation and visualization; and use mathematical processes to serve society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multi-step modeling projects and computational tools in curricula; assess problem formulation as well as solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal example: communication and resourcefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should read, write, listen, and speak mathematically; contribute to group efforts; communicate mathematics clearly; conduct research and make presentations; locate, analyze, synthesize, and evaluate information; and create/document algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess expository writing, oral presentations, group work, information literacy, and ethical awareness in mathematics contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal example: content-specific goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should understand theory and applications of calculus, basics of discrete mathematics and abstract algebra, and be able to write programs or use software with appropriate data structures to solve mathematical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map content goals to specific courses and include hands-on programming or software-based assignments where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design strategies: questions to ensure measurability and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: For each goal consider which parts of courses aim at the goal, what assignments help reach the goal, what students should do outside courses, what faculty should do, necessary facilities, and relevant learning-research findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to design strategies that both accomplish goals and produce evidence of student progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example strategy for proof-writing goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning goal: students should be able to read and understand mathematical statements, make and test conjectures, and construct/write proofs using a variety of methods and judge validity of complex arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: introduce theorems early, use counterexamples to motivate hypotheses, teach logic and proof techniques across years, require written and oral proofs, have mathematicians critique student work, and expose students to standard literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign responsibility and match methods to learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for each chosen area of assessment should be clearly assigned (e.g., mathematics faculty assess mathematics major), and assessment methods should reflect the type of learning to be measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with college/other units for shared responsibilities (e.g., core curriculum) and choose methods appropriate to each learning target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment method: Tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests can be objective or subjective, multiple-choice or free-response, written or oral, national/standardized or locally generated; effective for measuring specific knowledge and its basic meaning and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select test types aligned with what you want to measure (e.g., GRE for graduate preparation, local exams for course content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment method: Surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys (written or interviews) can target students, faculty, employers, and alumni about courses, majors, or reasons for changing majors; attitude surveys measure aptitudes like life-long learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys to capture perceptions, attitudes, and longitudinal information not accessible via tests or artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment method: Evaluation reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation reports use checklists of skills and abilities completed by faculty, peers, or employers (and sometimes self-evaluations) to evaluate individuals or groups; grades are fundamental evaluation reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these for holistic judgments of abilities; recognize limits of self-evaluation and complement with objective measures.
